reviews.content:
Those who shun conspiracy theorists are displaying their own narcissism “I just want that person back (for me)”. For any compassionate person these dark trends are vital to bring to awareness and enact change upon. 

Science spokespeople during covid gaslighted the public into feeling guilt and shame for making the rational point that we have immune systems that easily handle a flu like virus with a 99.9% survival rate, especially if treated with cheap, common and safe antivirals. Though there is no money in that therefore no incentive to affirm non-profitable scientific rigour. 

The government enforcement of an experimental vaccine that neither offered immunity nor safety fits the textbook definition of “abusive”. Lives have been destroyed not by a mild virus, but due to government overreach and the desperate ad-dollar funded media promoting a “safe and effective” treatment that was neither safe nor effective. Taxpayers will be paying off the covid debt decades into the future. “I was fine from my jab (therefore everyone else was too)” is pure narcissism and demonstrates low IQ all-or-nothing thinking. 

It’s well established that the CIA propagated the term ‘conspiracy theorist’ and that they purposefully promote hoax conspiracies to muddy the waters, distract from the true and evidenced conspiracies and discredit “the conspiracy movement” (there is no movement). All of these proofs are in their own archives open to the public. 

The solution to conspiracists is not to “save people” from realising truth according to your own standard of ignorance. It’s to boldly accept what the evidence is indicating, not live in wilful delusion. Vocalise your concern and solutions rationally, politely and hold yourself to a higher standard of intelligent inquiry. 

If you’d like to understand how the world really works consider listening to “coffee with Scott adams” podcast and join others who’ve become aware of our societal and institutional deceptions and how to navigate truthfully in this increasingly 1984ish reality.

reviews.author: Tate Causea
reviews.content:
Very disappointed in this episode. If I could give it zero I would. Biased is a word that applies here. 

To suggest that “conspiracy theorists” attract a certain type of individual with a certain type of ‘mentality’ is nonsense. It’s also insulting, especially to people who bother to listen, read and research contentious subject matter. 

For starters some conspiracies have turned out to be true, but lumping everyone together as conspiracy theorists is contempt prior to investigation. It’s prejudiced and judgemental. Having this attitude / approach is a much bigger problem than being a conspiracy theorist! It allows corruption to continue. 

Sure some conspiracies are just total garbage, but some definitely aren’t. Anyone with an ability to reason and think critically can understand this and tell the difference. 

It’s naive to think that scientific institutions, governments and every other set of power relations is going to be objective, transparent and honest. The reality is however that corruption exists everywhere, and it’s most commonly found in positions of power. “Power corrupts, and absolute power corrupts absolutely” as the quote goes.

reviews.author: Mollydoggles
reviews.content:
There was a lot of emphasis on how horrible having BPD is from the mental health sufferers side but little mentioned on how destructive and horrible it is to be at the very mercy of those with BPD. 
My workplace and my colleagues have suffered terribly from the utter ‘train wreck’ style that is working with a colleague with this diagnosis.From my experience there is very little understanding and empathy from those with BPD toward anyone else. And I DO NOT agree with that OT that the individual should conceal their diagnosis with management. 
How else can a workplace plan ahead for times of hostility and violent mood swings of the Staff member with BPD?
Sorry but that was a reckless comment.
Perhaps Sana, you could level the scales by having episodes that explore the experiences of those that live or work with someone with the multitude of mental health diagnoses you cover.
Couldn’t hurt seeing the issue from both sides.
See them as bookends.

reviews.author: zzzzz_1
reviews.content:
I really love this podcast. Sometimes it does brush over topics very broadly in a way that seemingly goes against its aims. 

The episode on attachment does the exact thing the podcast is criticising social media users of doing. Allowing a researcher to say that the concept of mental load appeared only a few years ago in public consciousness through a French cartoon in a blog is absurd. This absolutely ignores the long history of Feminist, black, queer and revolutionary work in this space. 

Bowlby was also not the first person to consider how the environment impacts a baby’s development - psychoanalysts had already been doing that for decades and Bowlby always acknowledged this. He was the first person to tie it to evolutionary biology.

Two very significant inconsistencies when you are claiming to set the record straight for all. 

Really love the podcast, but it is much more successful when it doesn’t have a snide tone.

reviews.author: Trexmonst
reviews.content: I get really concerned when “vanity” Is appealed to in order sell books. “High achievers” who chronically seek external validation and look at social media are in fact, garden variety insecure and anxious. It is INSUFFERABLE for a normal healthy actual high achiever ( without the vanity tag ) to be around people who whinge, compete look at social media like a teenager and seek praise. If your boss is a healthy person, your insecurity will reek ahead of you in any room you enter. And you will not become what your empty aspirations say you “should”. It’s pure vanity. Learn to self soothe. Learn to do a job without external gratification. Be quiet and get on with it without asking for prayer. Ughhh.

episodes.description: You think you know the story. You know how it ended. But you don’t know how it began. In the first episode of The Road to Bondi, reporter Josh Robertson traces the decades-long path that led a father and son to carry out their plan.

episodes.title: TRAILER — Introducing The Road to Bondi
episodes.description: In an ordinary Australian suburb, a father and son are secretly planning something terrible. One fateful summer evening, their path brings them crashing into the lives of strangers from around the world whose own stories haven’t yet been told.

episodes.title: 06 Hometown Boys | Not the only one
episodes.description: Insiders from the Harrow-Balmoral football club decide to break the code of silence. For Elise, it’s time to rebuild her life. But her story inspires other women to emerge with their own troubling accounts of the town’s club culture.

episodes.title: 05 Hometown Boys | 'Luke, Maybe'
episodes.description: A key witness submits a startling new statement that topples the guilty verdict and forces a retrial. This time, the men accused will not give evidence. But Lisa Hutchins, the trusted bush nurse will take the stand again — now for the defence.

episodes.title: 04 Hometown Boys | The Trial
episodes.description: As the criminal trial unfolds, witnesses from Balmoral waver on the stand, and the judge is "taken aback". The courtroom is heaving with supporters of the accused but the verdict is not what they're expecting.

reviews.author: NTAussie
reviews.content:
I listened to Background Briefing’s episode Hometown Boys with a heavy heart.

What happened to Elise was serious, devastating harm. Her experience, and the failures that allowed it to occur, deserve to be named clearly and held with honesty and accountability. My deepest sympathy is with Elise and her family, whose pain and loss should never be minimised or explained away.

I grew up in Balmoral, and my family has deep roots there also. It is a close-knit and caring community, even as it faces real and complex challenges today. That sense of connection and responsibility shaped me, I became a social worker because of that town.

I have two siblings with disability who were known, included, and valued growing up. People looked out for them. That experience also matters, and it too is part of Balmoral’s story.

While this episode powerfully highlighted harm and accountability, it felt like it reflected only a narrow subset of the community. Other voices and acts of care were largely absent, leaving the picture incomplete.

I hope future storytelling can hold more than one truth at once: the reality of profound harm, and the reality of communities that must reckon with it while still being capable of care, inclusion, and change

reviews.author: Sahpee
reviews.content:
It doesn’t matter if it’s a village in India, or a town in Victoria. After an horrific rape, the community prioritises the hierarchy and protecting the perpetrators. The community perpetuates the disgusting, criminal behaviour by gaslighting and bullying the victim instead of holding the perpetrators to account.
The victim and family pay over and over again throughout the fight for justice. These footy clubs are cesspools that perpetuate racism, violence, drink/drug culture, bullying and sexual violence, all carefully hidden under the thin veneer of sporting achievement. What hope do young boys have coming into this environment, especially if they live in the middle of nowhere and this club is the one option for social connection?

reviews.author: JacL25
reviews.content: Hometown Boys was a wonderful series. I hope it stops some people in their tracks to consider their response. This shows just how much a football club can influence the culture of a town. For the worse instead of better. Very few people showed courage and integrity in this ‘Elyce’ and her family showed  immense integrity and are the only ones who deserve to hold their head high. As a nurse I am disgusted in Lisa, advocating for the vulnerable is at the core of being a nurse……. You were misaligned with who were the vulnerable people here and i hope that the guilt you must feel is heavy to hold. This has shone a spotlight not only on Balmoral but on all small towns to consider what culture they have and what they stand for.

reviews.author: Samantha105
reviews.content: We live in a country where men are killing their partners frequently. I actually love Background briefing as a podcast, but wow this episode 2 of road to Bondi is almost mind boggling. Making excuses for a man who is in jail for assaulting (again) his pregnant partner because he ‘made some bad choices’ who is now going to be deported as he isn’t a citizen and continually ends up in jail, but oh - hang on we should treat him differently, because he was in the wrong place, at the wrong time - but did a good thing? I think this is what is exactly wrong with our legal system, and why people like him get chance, after chance, moving closer to the line before they cross over it. And someone dies….

reviews.author: Steph J C
reviews.content: Such a great podcast. Thank you to Elise for standing up and doing what a lot of women feel they can’t. It would have been incredibly tough to keep going and go to Court twice. You would no doubt have helped a lot of others in your situation for speaking out. Home Town Boys was really moving. She is incredibly strong and I just couldn’t believe her friends didn’t get up and get around her. What a traumatic experience she went through and to not have the support would have been so difficult. Also the courage of the few in the community that did speak out in support, hopefully more will stand up after listening to this.

reviews.author: Hoodooguru81
reviews.content:
Roy & HG mean the world to me.
They instantly transport me back to my childhood in the 80’s and 90’s where I would listen to them on Triple J whilst playing pool in my fathers shed as a young boy growing up in South West Sydney. 
Stepping into their world for an hour each week is something I hold dear, especially in this time when most are locked up in their homes. 
How does one sum up Roy and HG quickly? 
Think of stepping into the rabbit hole in Alice In Wonderland and entering into a magical world where too much sport is barely enough. A part truth, part fictional world that will leave you wondering have I entered the fifth dimension? 
Actually it’s more likened to tripping over a 6 foot divot left from a school fete tent in Watsford Oval, Lithgow. But you get the angle. 

Keep going as long as you can keep going guys. It is making a difference to many. 
Bless you both and Thankyou!

reviews.content: There are very few social commentators who capture the essence of the “Australian Monday Morning Sporting Experts” quite as insightfully as these two chaps. Long may they rule over the tracks, fields, pools, gymnasiums and change rooms of our young but great nation.

reviews.content: Gentlemen I’ve followed your antics for years as I ‘bludged’ on my way to training for (and winning) Aussie Gold in aerobics, through marathon training, travelling home from underwater hockey training, hours of surf boat training and learning rugby. I _love_ that these days women get at least an occasional mention. In the beginning I found myself shouting at the radio a bit as you lamented poor performances by Aussie men, but women weren’t mentioned. Glad times are changing

reviews.author: Water bus
reviews.content:
I respect Geraldine and Hamish as journalists but I don’t really want to hear their opinions and interpretations on world affairs for 5 minutes at the start and end of the podcast. Maybe Geraldine and Hamish would argue they’re “contextualising” the topic at hand but I tend to think they just use the time to give their own opinions and interpretation of the topic.
Cutting the opinion segments would enable a longer interview with the guests - and currently the interviews are too short especially given there’s two hosts trying to ask questions. 

The choice of guests also tends to be lacking in originality and generally only offers a Western centric pro-US view of the world, mainly interviewing people from the the foreign policy establishment (eg Chatham House, anti-Trump commentators etc). I wouldn’t mind this if the guests got asked critical questions challenging their arguments and logic, but unfortunately Geraldine and Hamish’s questions tend to be very vague, which means we don’t get much of a stimulating debate. Also you can just turn on the tv and radio and hear the same kinds of establishment views so what is Global Roaming offering that’s new or different?

Interviewing Kishore Mahbubani and Hugh White is a good start as they think a bit differently to the Western establishment, but again the interviews were pretty short and tended to have unfocused, long-winded questions like asking Mahbubani about whether democracy has innate strengths, and I’m just not sure why that was relevant to the bigger picture of the Asian century and the changing international environment.

It’s good that the abc still has a podcast like this dedicated to international politics but I think the podcast could make a fair few improvements.

reviews.content: The GR team’s recent summer series on the Aukus debacle is a rare exception in the Australian media landscape of in-depth analysis of the pure folly of the Aukus announcement, and the disastrous impact it has had on Australia’s relationships with its immediate neighbours and its biggest trading partner China. The Aukus ‘deal’, which was foisted on the long-suffering Australian public by former Prime Minister Morrison in a media stunt with outgoing US President Joe Biden and former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson in 2022, and then adopted in unseemly haste (following a 2 hour consideration by shadow Cabinet) by the then Labor Opposition, has not faced any serious scrutiny in the largely pro-Washington mainstream media in Australia, but there have been some low-level questions asked (for example by Australian Greens Senator David Shoebridge during Senate Estimates), and some excellent books and journal articles investigating the shadowy figures who brought the ‘deal’ to fruition, and some, like former Prime Ministers Turnbull and Keating, querying the wisdom of the  whole thing. ‘deal’

reviews.author: Primary_Persephone
reviews.content:
I really value the perspective that Geraldine brings to the podcast. One of the reasons I am a regular listener of the pod is because it isn’t an echo chamber - the conversations challenge assumptions and encourage people to think more deeply about complex global issues.

Her comment about the Iranian people needing to find a way to rise up / find a solution has attracted criticism - and quite a strong response from Hamish- but I think it was pointing to a broader historial reality: meaningful and sustainable political change often has to come from within societies themselves. Acknowledging that doesn’t ignore the enormous risks that people face under authoritarian regimes nor does it dismiss the incredible courage shown by many Iranians. 

Thanks Geraldine and Hamish for creating the space for this types of conversations - especially in a time where people have lost the ability to disagree constructively. It’s appreciated.

reviews.author: Easybreather13
reviews.content:
Philip Adams is unashamedly atheist and very much firmly ensconced on the left side of politics. So he is bound to infuriate those equally ensconced in the opposite camps of politics and belief. However for an agnostic, swing voter like myself, he represents a most rare and precious reminder of the potential of the mass media to inform and challenge rather than simply reinforce prejudice and and preexisting belief. When one compares the shrill but disingenuous moral indignation of the parrots of talkback radio, Mr Adams is clearly operating in a much higher league thereby reminding us of how much potential radio programs of this nature really have. 

With  his calm but cynical tone, his superb wit, eloquence and sense of humour, it is hard not to enjoy and relish this wonderful “ little wireless program” of Mr Adams. He regularly has some excellent guests however ultimately it is Mr Adams to whom I find myself drawn. Wherever one sits on the political spectrum few would deny that Philip Adams is a now one of Australia’s most perceptive and experienced journalists. His apparently sincere concerns for social justice, and his willingness to consider new facts and ideas contrasts with the dogmatic  sophistry of the  shock jocks of mostly conservative talkback radio. However it is worth reminding onself that he does not have a monopoly on common sense and his rigid view on God and politics should be regarded with some circumspection

reviews.author: RobnJPerthAus
reviews.content:
I'll start with what would usually be an entire review, or the last line of a review: definitely worth a listen.

Stories of people embroiled in scientific endeavours; Stories from people's lives, understood through science; & Science's uncertainties (or are they?) presented for us to think on and maybe, act on.

The maker of this program (the host, who seems to be at the helm of this program) has combined her scientific credentials with her years in radio gathering & telling stories. This podcast feels like the culmination of all she's done so far, with the result being really interesting stories that come out of science.

From the enthralling first episode of amazing storytelling about some *epic* science, to the final episode of the first season about some very close-to-home science that will send many to the Science Friction website looking for more information, this podcast is the stuff of legends and the stories around the evidence of science.

The episodes are a good length, starting with a couple around 35 minutes to accomodate the dramatic & profound stories they tell. Then it's down to shorter episodes, packed with enough science to give you the guts of it in digestible terms, surrounded by the stories that relate the science firmly to the experiences of people.

Sometimes a story is of a scientific field that's relatively new but widely accepted, or as in the final episode, science that has been debated for years. And not just debated because science is progressed by further findings that support (or don't), expand, or contest what has come before. We hear the differing views of scientists working on research into the same issue - and that's excluding the interest groups that have an agenda for one outcome to be "the right outcome". But they're represented too: in the last episode of season one, an industry group who chose not to be interviewed provide their statement for us to read.

I usually wanted to get more of an understanding on topics covered, sometimes out of interest, and sometimes because I had a decision to make: was there evidence that would lead me to change my behaviour or decisions? Episode 6, as I mentioned, is an example of that & will have many heading to the website with their questions. And there are different answers for everyone depending on their circumstances and their response to what's presented.

And, as the host says, there's the rub.

@RobnWithAWhy

title: A Death In Cryptoland - ABC listen
description: When the young CEO of Canada's largest cryptocurrency exchange is reported to have died while honeymooning in India, it sets off a cataclysmic chain of events that would leave about 76,000 people out of a quarter of a billion dollars and a trail of conspiracy theories around whether Gerald Cotten is dead or alive. A Death in Cryptoland is an original podcast series about a crypto-tycoon, his secret past, his sudden demise, and an online sleuth's obsession to unravel the truth behind QuadrigaCX. Hosted by Takara Small.

episodes.title: 01 | The Body
episodes.description: Upon checking into a luxury resort in India, Gerald Cotten complains to the staff that he's feeling ill. He and his wife are taken to a hospital and within 24 hours, the young CEO is declared dead.

episodes.title: 02 | Hunting Ghosts
episodes.description: QuadrigaCX collapses and there's widespread panic. An online sleuth searches for answers through a tangle of websites, hidden identities and a trail of emails.

episodes.title: 03 | Cracks in the Empire
episodes.description: Gerald Cotten and his business partner, Michael Patryn, launch QuadrigaCX on Boxing Day, 2013. There's hype in the budding Bitcoin community and the small exchange seems to have a meteoric rise.

episodes.title: 04 | Voleur
episodes.description: Despite Michael Patryn's denials that he's a fraudster named Omar Dhanani, customers aren't buying it. They're demanding proof. A mugshot.

episodes.title: 05 | Where's the Money Gerry?
episodes.description: As financial investigators struggle to find any of the missing quarter of a billion dollars, they begin to make some bizarre discoveries around how the exchange had operated — finding funny business from the very start.

episodes.title: 06 | The End Game
episodes.description: The revelation that Gerry's house of cards had been falling apart — just as he's reported dead in India — leaves people wondering: is this an exit scheme? Could Gerry still be alive?

reviews.author: Grand poo bar
reviews.content: This subject matter is interesting but I swear to G this podcast could have been one episode and is fairly awfully researched and written. The narrator cuts over the top of interviewees frequently with useless musings and they don’t explain the most interesting parts of this story to spend too much time on mundane details. They also skip over and mention in passing the most interesting and key theories about this case in the last episode! Waste of time. Find an article and read about it.
